articles.content_excerpt: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Early voting opened here in Idaho on October 19, and we were among the first to go in and exercise our franchise. The ballot this time includes four measures for voters to consider. One is an invitation to designate the official state gun. Choices include one modern rifle, two World War II icons, and three Wild West classics. In a state where six of every ten people own guns, this measure is not surprising. The others are less frivolous. Two of them would amend the state constitution in consequential ways. articles.title: Hell Is Real
articles.author: Eva Amar
articles.content_excerpt: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. In 2010, I was driving along Interstate 65 toward Bloomington, Indiana, when an enormous roadside billboard caught my attention. HELL IS REAL. I was returning to Indiana University, where my daughter had been raped four years earlier. Of all the messages I might have encountered along that highway, those three words seemed almost deliberately placed in my path. Back in the mid-1970s, when I worked as a systems support technician, my colleagues nicknamed me “Queen Irony.” If I said the sky was blue, it would almost immediately turn black and start pouring. articles.title: Generation Revolts Against Capitalism
articles.author: Henry A. Giroux
articles.content_excerpt: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Across France, Spain, India, Italy, Albania, and other parts of the world, young people are taking to the streets, giving voice to a growing international revolt against the collapse of social protections, the underfunding of education, the erosion of democratic rights, and the cruel politics of austerity. Despite their different national histories, these struggles share a growing anger at the savage machinery of neoliberal capitalism, its abandonment of the young, its concentration of wealth and power in the hands of ruling elites, its embrace of militarism, and its systematic destruction of the public institutions and social protections on which democratic life depends. articles.title: Adolph Reed on What It Will Take to Defeat Trumpism
articles.author: Adolph Reed
articles.content_excerpt: With the 2026 midterm elections approaching and Donald Trump’s approval ratings at record lows , it’s easy to hope that we might someday soon find the politics of Trumpism behind us. But it’s far from clear that the Democratic Party can effectively capitalize on anti-Trump sentiment, and Democrats certainly are not offering a clear, compelling program that could address widespread political discontent. In a wide-ranging interview with the European Center for Populism Studies’s Selcuk Gultasli, political scientist and longtime socialist organizer Adolph Reed Jr offers a political-economic interpretation of Trumpism, arguing that the structural contradictions underlying authoritarian nationalism remain fundamentally unresolved. articles.title: Israel’s Election Offers a Bleak Future for the Palestinians
articles.author: Ambra Suriano
articles.content_excerpt: Israel’s parliamentary elections are fast approaching on October 27, with Benjamin Netanyahu facing a challenge from the opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot. Netanyahu is backed by a coalition of religious ultranationalist parties, while Eisenkot advocates a more liberal or secular form of Zionism, pledging to achieve what his party describes as a Zionist goal: “to make Israel, by 2048, a prosperous model state — a source of pride, built on partnership, fellowship and mutual responsibility.” But what would a victory for either bloc mean for Palestinian society in the West Bank and the Gaza Strip? Unfortunately, whoever wins the election, there is not going to be any change to Israel’s denial of basic rights to the Palestinian people. articles.title: Natural Progress and the Gilded Age: A Review of Our Kindred Creatures
articles.author: Rochester Red Star: News from Rochester DSA
articles.content_excerpt: by Travis Covitz Combining my long-standing interest in animal welfare with Gilded Age politics, Our Kindred Creatures: How Americans Came to Feel the Way They Do About Animals by Bill Wasik and Monica Murphy caught my eye at the local library. This 2024 book explores the rise of the American animal welfare movement from the 1860s through the 1890s, looking at pets, livestock, scientific research, wildlife, circuses, and more. Although I was frequently underwhelmed with the politics of the authors, I found this book quite thought-provoking. It is absolutely true that the relationship between the average American and different animals has completely transformed in the past 150 years. articles.title: UAW Members at Triumph Group Vote 99% to Authorize Strike
articles.author: Justin Mayhugh
articles.content_excerpt: After a two-day vote, UAW Local 405 members at Triumph Group who make engine controls and other components for U.S. military aircrafts voted 99% (148-1 with 86% turning out) in favor of authorizing a strike for any time after the current union contract expires at midnight on October 31. Core demands include sectoral standard wages, job security, cost-of-living protection, affordable healthcare and no concessions, among other priority issues the company has not even attempted to meet the bargaining committee on. “This vote should send a clear message to Triumph Group that UAW Local 405 members are not settling for their abysmal proposals,” said UAW Region 9A Director Brandon Mancilla. “During the life of our last contract, Triumph Group made $680 million off the work of these members. Retired probation officer Diana Salcedo had downsized to a home in Imperial’s Paseo del Sol neighborhood and was looking forward to a new chapter in her life caring for her mother and young grandchildren. articles.author: Gabriel Thompson
articles.content_excerpt: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. On a sunny September afternoon, Juan Carlos stands behind the counter of his compact variety shop in California’s Central Valley, notes the lack of customers and pulls out a binder full of questions. During breaks, the slender 47-year-old is studying for his U.S. citizenship test. articles.title: Medicaid Cuts Pose Political Risk for Six-Term Congressman
articles.author: Elizabeth Aguilera
articles.content_excerpt: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Danielle Velling depends on monthly injections to keep her severe asthma at bay in California’s Central Valley, one of the most polluted regions in the U.S., where asthma rates exceed those in other parts of the state. She receives the medication thanks to Medicaid, the government-funded insurance program, known in California as Medi-Cal. But now she worries she could lose that insurance. Concern about cuts to health care prompted Velling, and dozens of others, to spend a record hot evening last month campaigning for upstart Democrat Randy Villegas. articles.author: William J. Astore
articles.content_excerpt: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Donald Trump is a one-man horror show. Call him “annihilation man” for threatening to exterminate nearly 93 million Iranians for the crime of defying his will (and that of Israel and Netanyahu). I don’t write about Trump a lot because he’s so scrutable. He is what he is, an utterly shameless con man, a bullying narcissist who’s always on the make. What he isn’t, what he’s never been, what he never will be, is a public servant. Sadly, he has a lot of company. articles.title: A New Israeli Government Won’t Stop the Settlements
articles.author: Diana Buttu
articles.content_excerpt: Next Tuesday, Israel will hold its first general election since the October 7 attacks and the destruction of Gaza. The election campaign has again illustrated the radicalization of Israeli politics, even beyond Benjamin Netanyahu’s government, and the breadth of political forces who staunchly resist the creation of a Palestinian state. In an interview, Palestinian Canadian lawyer and analyst Diana Buttu, who lives in Haifa, explains why she will cast her ballot in this election while rejecting Israel’s claim to be a democracy. Speaking to Elias Feroz for Jacobin , she discusses what a change of government could — and could not — mean for Palestinians, the new death penalty law, and the planned Palestinian elections next month.
